title: SHADDAI Game Forge
text:
# SHADDAI Game Forge

SHADDAI's own toolkit for building browser games — 3D (Three.js) and 2D. Reached through the MCP by TURTLE (`shaddai_turtle_build`) and by anyone via `gamedev_search`.

## What's here
| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `ecs/world.mjs` | Entity-component-system: generational handles, sparse-set storage, cached queries, phases, deferred changes, events (tested) |
| `runtime/fixed-step.mjs` | Fixed-timestep loop with interpolation and stall protection |
| `runtime/collide.mjs` | Box sweeps with automatic sub-stepping, sliding response, ray casts |
| `runtime/clips.mjs` | Sprite sheets and time-driven animation clips |
| `runtime/actions.mjs` | Input buffering, coyote-time-style forgiveness, axes |
| `guides/01–11` | Scene setup, the loop, cameras and feel, assets and materials, shaders, physics, ECS, 2D sprites, performance, running a project, release QA |

## Use it
```
node ecs/world.test.mjs
node runtime/runtime.test.mjs
```
Both suites must pass before anything here changes.

## Reading order
Starting a 3D game: 01 → 02 → 03 → 04 → 06 → 07 → 09.  
Starting a 2D game: 02 → 03 → 08 → 06 → 07 → 09.  
Running the project: 10 then 11.

## Principles
- Gameplay is a pure function of a fixed clock — replayable, testable, the same on every device.
- The scene is a view of game state, never the source of truth.
- Measure before optimising; ship a quality ladder, not one setting.
- Feel (guide 03) comes before content.

title: Provenance
text:
# Provenance

Game Forge — code, guides and tests — was written for SHADDAI from first principles. It does not contain files, text or code from any other project. Game-development techniques (fixed timesteps, sparse sets, swept collision, spring cameras, sprite clips, etc.) are general engineering knowledge.

title: 02 · The game loop
text:
# 02 · The game loop

Rendering speed varies by device; game rules must not. Separate them.

## The rule
**Simulate in fixed slices. Render whenever the browser says so, blending between the last two simulated states.**

`runtime/fixed-step.mjs` does this:
```js
import { FixedStep, blend } from './runtime/fixed-step.mjs';

const loop = new FixedStep({
  hz: 60,
  update: (dt) => world.step(dt),          // always 1/60 s
  render: (alpha) => {                     // 0..1 progress to the next slice
    for (const m of movers) m.mesh.position.x = blend(m.prevX, m.x, alpha);
    renderer.render(scene, camera);
  },
});
renderer.setAnimationLoop((ms) => loop.tick(ms / 1000));
```

## Why it matters
- **Same behaviour everywhere.** A 144 Hz laptop and a 30 Hz phone get identical physics and identical replays.
- **Stable physics.** Integrators and collision resolve badly with wildly varying `dt`.
- **Deterministic tests.** Feed 600 ticks into the world and assert the result — no browser needed.

## Stall protection
Tabs pause. Debuggers pause. Without a cap the loop returns after a minute and tries to simulate 3,600 steps at once. `maxCatchUp` (default 0.25 s) drops the backlog instead. Pair it with the Page Visibility API: pause audio and timers on `visibilitychange`.

## Store previous state
For interpolation, each mover needs `prev` and `curr`. Copy `curr → prev` at the **start** of each update, then integrate. Teleports (respawns) should set both so the mesh doesn't streak across the map.

## Time you can trust
- Use the simulation clock (`world.time`) for gameplay timers: cooldowns, spawn waves, status effects.
- Use the wall clock only for presentation: UI fades, camera shake decay, particle lifetime.
- Never use `Date.now()` for gameplay; it breaks pause and replay.

## Slow-motion and pause
Scale `dt` before it reaches `world.step` (`dt * timeScale`). Pausing is `timeScale = 0`; the render side keeps drawing, so menus and camera still animate.

title: 06 · Physics and collision
text:
# 06 · Physics and collision

Pick the lightest tool that gives the behaviour you need.

| Your game needs | Use | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Platformer, top-down, blocky worlds | **Box sweeps** (`runtime/collide.mjs`) | Tiny |
| Picking, line of sight, ground checks | **Ray casts** | Tiny |
| Stacking crates, rolling balls, ragdolls | A full rigid-body engine (WASM) | Significant |
| Vehicles, joints, constraints | A full rigid-body engine | Significant |

Most games never need the last two. Reach for a heavy engine only when stacking, tumbling or joints are core to the fun.

## Character controllers (platformers)
Use a **kinematic** controller: you decide velocity, the collision code only stops you. Don't make the player a free-tumbling rigid body.
```js
body.vy -= GRAVITY * dt;                        // 30–40 u/s² feels punchy; real gravity feels floaty
body.vy = Math.max(body.vy, -TERMINAL);
const { box, hit } = moveAndSlide(body, { x: body.vx * dt, y: body.vy * dt }, solids);
Object.assign(body, box);
if (hit.y) { if (body.vy < 0) grounded = true; body.vy = 0; }
if (hit.x) body.vx = 0;
```
Add **variable jump height** (cut `vy` when the button is released early), **coyote time** and a **jump buffer** (`runtime/actions.mjs`). These three change feel more than any physics tuning.

## Broad phase when you have many bodies
Brute-force overlap tests are fine below ~100 bodies. Beyond that, bucket bodies into a uniform grid keyed by cell (`Math.floor(x / cell)`), and only test neighbours in the same or adjacent cells.

## Tunnelling
A fast body can skip entirely over a thin wall between two frames. `moveAndSlide` sub-steps automatically. For projectiles, ray cast along the path travelled this tick instead of testing the end position.

## Determinism
Fixed timestep (guide 02) + no `Math.random` in physics + a fixed iteration order = identical results on every machine. That unlocks replays, rollback netcode, and reliable automated tests.

## Debug it visually
Draw every collider as a wireframe box in a toggleable layer. Most "physics bugs" are a collider that isn't where you think it is.

title: 11 · Release QA checklist
text:
# 11 · Release QA checklist

Run top to bottom before any build goes to players. Record pass/fail and the build id.

## Plays right
- [ ] New player reaches the first goal without help in under 2 minutes
- [ ] Every verb has visual, audio and (where relevant) haptic feedback
- [ ] Death/failure restarts in under 3 seconds
- [ ] No soft-locks: try to get stuck on purpose in each level
- [ ] Difficulty curve: the first 5 minutes are easy, the rest escalates

## Runs right
- [ ] Holds target frame rate on the slowest supported device (low preset)
- [ ] No frame-time spikes over 50 ms during normal play
- [ ] Memory stays flat over a 30-minute session (no leak growth)
- [ ] Loading time under 5 s on a mid-range connection; progress is shown
- [ ] Tab hidden → returns without a burst of catch-up or stuck audio

## Works everywhere
- [ ] Latest Chrome, Safari, Firefox, and one mobile browser
- [ ] Window resize, orientation change, DPR change handled
- [ ] Keyboard, mouse, touch and (if promised) gamepad all work; no stuck keys after focus loss
- [ ] Remappable or at least discoverable controls

## Accessible
- [ ] Text readable at phone size; contrast meets WCAG AA
- [ ] Information never carried by colour alone
- [ ] Sound is not required to play; subtitles for spoken lines
- [ ] Reduce-motion option disables shake, flashes and parallax
- [ ] No flashing faster than 3 times per second

## Safe
- [ ] Client is never trusted for scores, currency or unlocks — the server validates
- [ ] Inputs sanitised; saves can't be edited to crash or grant rewards
- [ ] No secrets or API keys in shipped code
- [ ] Rate limits on anything that costs money or hits an external service
- [ ] Privacy: only collect what's needed; say what and why

## Release hygiene
- [ ] Version number visible in the menu
- [ ] Error reporting wired; test error shows up
- [ ] Rollback plan: the previous build is one step away
- [ ] Known issues list written, even if short

## Automated checks worth having
- Deterministic simulation test: run N ticks from a seed, assert a hash of final state.
- Collision unit tests (floors, walls, corners, fast movers).
- A "monkey" run: random inputs for 5 minutes must not crash.

title: 03 · Cameras and game feel
text:
# 03 · Cameras and game feel

A camera is a character. Players judge a game's quality within seconds largely by how it moves.

## Follow camera with smoothing that doesn't lag
Plain `lerp(camera, target, 0.1)` is frame-rate dependent: it feels different at 30 and 144 fps. Use an exponential decay instead:

```js
// k = how quickly we close the gap (per second). 6–12 feels snappy, 2–4 feels floaty.
const damp = (current, target, k, dt) => target + (current - target) * Math.exp(-k * dt);

camera.position.x = damp(camera.position.x, player.x + offset.x, 8, dt);
camera.position.y = damp(camera.position.y, player.y + offset.y, 5, dt);   // slower on Y = less nausea
camera.position.z = damp(camera.position.z, player.z + offset.z, 8, dt);
camera.lookAt(player.x, player.y + 1, player.z);
```

## Look-ahead
Shift the focus point toward where the player is *going*: `focus = player + velocity * 0.25`. The player sees more of what's coming; the camera feels intelligent.

## Dead zone
In 2D and side-scrollers, let the player move inside a small box before the camera follows. Constant tracking makes tiny movements feel jittery.

## Collision-aware third-person
Cast a ray from the player's head to the desired camera spot (`collide.mjs → raycast`). If it hits geometry, put the camera just in front of the hit. Ease back out slowly once the view clears.

## Shake that reads as impact
```js
// trauma ∈ [0,1], raised by hits and decayed over time; shake grows with trauma².
const s = trauma * trauma;
camera.rotation.z = s * 0.05 * noise(t * 30);
camera.position.x += s * 0.3 * noise(t * 27 + 10);
trauma = Math.max(0, trauma - dt * 1.4);
```
Use smooth noise, not `Math.random()`, or the shake looks like static. Shake rotation more than position.

## Juice checklist (do these before adding content)
- **Hit stop:** freeze the simulation 50–90 ms on a heavy hit.
- **Squash and stretch:** scale the sprite or mesh 10–20% on jump and landing, restoring over ~120 ms.
- **Input forgiveness:** buffer presses and allow coyote time (`runtime/actions.mjs`).
- **Audio on every verb:** jump, land, hit, pickup. Silence reads as broken.
- **Particles on contact:** a few short-lived puffs sell weight.
- **FOV kick:** widen the field of view 3–6° when sprinting; ease it back.

title: 12 · Animation
08 · 2D sprites and animation
text:
# 08 · 2D sprites and animation

## Sheet layout
Put a character's frames in a **grid**: one row per action (idle, walk, jump, attack), one column per frame. Equal cell size, transparent background, feet on the same baseline in every frame so the character doesn't bob when clips switch.

```js
import { gridSheet, clip } from './runtime/clips.mjs';
const sheet = gridSheet({ cols: 8, rows: 4, frameW: 64, frameH: 64 });
const clips = {
  idle:   clip(sheet, { row: 0, from: 0, to: 3, fps: 6,  mode: 'loop' }),
  run:    clip(sheet, { row: 1, from: 0, to: 7, fps: 14, mode: 'loop' }),
  attack: clip(sheet, { row: 2, from: 0, to: 5, fps: 18, mode: 'once' }),
};
const frame = clips[state].at(timeInState);        // → { x, y, w, h, u, v, uw, vh }
```
Clips are pure functions of time, so pausing, slow-motion and replay need no extra state.

## Drawing
- **Canvas 2D:** `ctx.drawImage(img, f.x, f.y, f.w, f.h, dx, dy, f.w, f.h)`; set `ctx.imageSmoothingEnabled = false` for crisp pixel art.
- **three.js:** a plane with a `MeshBasicMaterial`, `transparent: true`; set the texture's `repeat` to `(f.uw, f.vh)` and `offset` to `(f.u, f.v)`. Use `NearestFilter` for pixel art.

## State machine, not flags
Drive the clip from a state (`idle → run → jump → fall → land`). On state change reset `timeInState` to 0. Transitions are explicit; no tangle of booleans.

## Timing feel
- 8–14 fps reads as hand-drawn and charming; 24+ looks smooth but costs more art.
- Hold the **contact frame** of attacks a beat longer; it sells impact more than extra frames do.
- Anticipation (a small wind-up) + follow-through (a settle) matter more than frame count.

## Pixel art at any screen size
Render the game at a small fixed resolution (e.g. 320×180) and scale the canvas by an **integer** factor. Non-integer scaling shimmers.

## Layering
Draw by **y-order** in top-down games (lower on screen = in front). Separate parallax layers move at fractions of camera speed (far = 0.2, mid = 0.5, near = 1.0).

## Production tips
- Keep a source layered file per character; export sheets by script so a tweak is one command.
- Name clips consistently across characters (`idle`, `run`, `attack`) so the same controller code drives any of them.
- Generated art needs the same checks as hand-drawn: consistent baseline, consistent palette, no stray edge pixels.

title: 04 · Assets, lighting and materials
text:
# 04 · Assets, lighting and materials

## Formats
| Need | Use | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 3D models | **glTF / GLB** | The web standard; carries meshes, materials, skeletons, animations |
| Small downloads | Draco or meshopt compression | Compress geometry once at build time |
| GPU-friendly textures | **KTX2 (Basis)** | Stays compressed in video memory; JPG/PNG expand to full size |
| Sprites | PNG sheets or WebP | Keep power-of-two atlas dimensions for mipmaps |
| Audio | OGG/AAC for music, short WAV/OGG for effects | Decode effects once, keep buffers |

## Loading without a stall
- Show a loading screen driven by a real progress counter (`LoadingManager`).
- Load in tiers: **boot** (menu, player), **level** (current area), **stream** (next area, decorative props).
- Cache by URL. Two requests for the same file should share one promise.
- Decode off the main thread where possible (`ImageBitmapLoader`, worker-based KTX2/Draco decoders).

```js
const cache = new Map();
export const load = (url, loader) =>
  cache.get(url) ?? cache.set(url, loader.loadAsync(url)).get(url);
```

## Materials: pick the cheapest that looks right
1. **MeshBasicMaterial** — unlit. Free. Great for UI planes, skyboxes, stylised flat looks.
2. **MeshLambertMaterial** — cheap diffuse lighting.
3. **MeshStandardMaterial** — physically based; use for hero assets.
4. **ShaderMaterial** — custom look (guide 05) when the built-ins can't do it.

Share material instances between meshes. Fifty crates with fifty identical materials cost fifty draw states; one shared material is one.

## Lighting for games
- **One key light** (directional) + **a hemisphere or ambient fill**. More lights = more shader cost per pixel.
- Bake what never moves: lightmaps and baked AO beat dynamic lights for static scenery.
- Environment maps (a small HDR) make Standard materials look right with almost no extra lights.
- Cheap fake shadows (a dark blob decal under characters) are fine for crowds.

## Colour discipline
Colour textures (albedo/emissive) are sRGB; data textures (normal, roughness, metalness, AO) are linear. Mixing them up is the number-one reason "the colours look wrong".

## Instancing
Many copies of one mesh? `InstancedMesh` draws thousands in a single call. Update per-instance transforms with `setMatrixAt` and flag `instanceMatrix.needsUpdate = true` once per frame, not per instance.

title: 10 · Running a game project
text:
# 10 · Running a game project

A small game is a sequence of decisions made in a good order. This is SHADDAI's order.

## Roles (people or agents)
| Role | Owns | SHADDAI agent |
|---|---|---|
| Director | the one-sentence pitch, scope, final call | SHADDAI |
| Engineer | loop, systems, tools, performance | NEXUS |
| Designer | rules, balance, level flow, onboarding | ORACLE |
| Artist | look, characters, UI, animation | TURTLE |
| Writer | text, tutorials, store copy | QUILL |
| QA / security | breakage, exploits, cheating, privacy | PIKADON |
| Economy | pricing, rewards, sinks and sources | ZEROX |

One person can wear several hats. The point is that every decision has an owner.

## Gates — don't skip a gate to save a day
1. **Pitch.** One sentence: *who* does *what* and why it's fun. If it needs two sentences it is two games.
2. **Core loop prototype.** Grey boxes, one mechanic, 30 seconds of play. If this isn't fun, stop or change it; art can't rescue it.
3. **Vertical slice.** One short level at final quality — art, sound, UI, feel. It sets the bar for everything else.
4. **Content pass.** Build the remaining levels, enemies and items using the systems the slice proved.
5. **Polish and balance.** Feel, difficulty curve, onboarding, performance ladder.
6. **Release candidate.** Feature freeze. Only fixes. Run the QA checklist (guide 11).
7. **Ship and listen.** Instrument it, read feedback, patch in small steps.

## Design document: one page
- Pitch (one sentence) · target player · platform and input
- Core loop (verbs → feedback → goal)
- Failure and restart (how quickly, how kindly)
- Progression (what changes over time)
- Scope list: **must**, **should**, **could**. Cut from the bottom first.
- Risks (the three things most likely to sink it) and how you'll test each early

## Scope control
- Estimate in days, then double it.
- Every new idea goes on the "could" list, not into the build.
- A feature that needs a new system, new art and new UI at once is three features.

## Playtesting
Watch someone play without helping. Note where they hesitate, where they laugh, where they quit. Five players find most problems. Fix the problem you saw, not the solution they suggested.

## Working with agents
Give each agent a role, a gate, and a definition of done. Hand work over as files (design doc, shot list, asset list), not chat. Have a different agent review than the one that built.

title: 15 · Post-processing and finishing
text:
# 15 · Post-processing and finishing

Post-processing renders the scene to an off-screen image, then runs full-screen passes over it. It's the cheapest way to give a game a *look* — and the easiest way to wreck performance, because every pass touches every pixel.

## Pipeline shape
```
scene → render target → [bloom] → [colour grade] → [vignette] → [anti-alias / output] → screen
```
Use an effect-composer style chain: one render pass, then your effects, then an output pass that handles tone mapping and colour space once.

## Effects worth having
| Effect | What it sells | Cost | Tip |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bloom** | glow on lights, magic, UI emissives | medium | Raise the *threshold* so only bright things bloom; low strength, wide radius |
| **Colour grading** | mood and cohesion | cheap | A tiny 3D LUT or three sliders (contrast, saturation, tint) |
| **Vignette** | focus, cinematic frame | cheap | Keep it subtle (≤0.25) |
| **Outline** | readable silhouettes, stylised look | medium | Depth/normal edge detection; skip on mobile |
| **Depth of field** | scale and focus | expensive | Prefer fake blur on backgrounds |
| **Chromatic aberration / film grain** | impact flashes, texture | cheap | Pulse on hits, not constant |
| **FXAA/SMAA** | smooth edges when MSAA is off | cheap | Use when post-processing disables native antialiasing |

## Rules
1. **Budget passes.** Each full-screen pass costs roughly one more screen's worth of pixel work. On low quality, run none or one.
2. **Render at lower resolution** for expensive passes (bloom works fine at half resolution).
3. **Do tone mapping once**, at the end, not in each pass.
4. **Make effects driven by game state:** brief bloom/aberration spikes on explosions, desaturation at low health, tint by biome. Static filters get ignored; reactive ones get noticed.
5. **Always provide a toggle** (accessibility and performance): reduce-motion disables flashes, shake and aberration.

## Cheaper alternatives
- Fake glow: an additive, softly-textured quad behind bright objects.
- Fake fog: scene `Fog` or a gradient to the sky colour — one line, no pass.
- Baked colour: bake grading into textures and lighting for static scenes.

## Check list before shipping a look
- Looks right on both dark and bright scenes.
- Text and UI stay crisp (draw UI after post-processing or in HTML).
- Frame time with effects on stays inside the quality ladder (guide 09).

title: 13 · Geometry and textures
text:
# 13 · Geometry and textures

## Geometry
A mesh is a list of vertices plus triangles (indices). Built-ins (`BoxGeometry`, `SphereGeometry`, `PlaneGeometry`, `CylinderGeometry`) cover prototypes. Build your own with `BufferGeometry`:

```js
const geo = new THREE.BufferGeometry();
geo.setAttribute('position', new THREE.Float32BufferAttribute([0,0,0,  1,0,0,  0,1,0], 3));
geo.setAttribute('uv',       new THREE.Float32BufferAttribute([0,0,  1,0,  0,1], 2));
geo.setIndex([0, 1, 2]);
geo.computeVertexNormals();
```

### Rules of thumb
- Segment counts: spheres rarely need more than 32×16; flat planes need 1×1 unless you displace them.
- **Merge** static scenery into few meshes; **instance** repeated props.
- Update vertex data sparingly: set `attribute.needsUpdate = true` once per frame at most, and prefer doing motion in a vertex shader.
- Recentre geometry (`geo.center()`) so rotation pivots where you expect.
- Bounding volumes drive culling; after changing vertices call `geo.computeBoundingSphere()`.

## Procedural worlds
Heightmap terrain: a subdivided plane whose vertex `y` comes from layered noise (`sum of noise(x·f)·a` for a few octaves). Chunk it (e.g. 64×64 tiles) so you can build, hide and dispose by region.

## Textures
| Kind | Colour space | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Albedo / emissive | sRGB | what you see |
| Normal, roughness, metalness, AO | Linear | raw data — never colour-managed |

- **Mipmaps** on (default) for anything that shrinks with distance; off for UI and pixel art.
- **Anisotropy** (`texture.anisotropy = 4`) sharpens textures seen at grazing angles, like floors.
- Pixel art: `magFilter = minFilter = NearestFilter`, no mipmaps.
- Tiling: `wrapS = wrapT = RepeatWrapping`, then set `repeat`.
- Pack channels: store roughness, metalness and AO in one texture's R/G/B to cut texture reads.

## Atlases
One big texture with many sub-images means one material and one draw call. Offset UVs per sprite or tile; leave 1–2 px padding between cells to prevent bleeding when filtered.

## Generated textures
Draw to a small `<canvas>` and wrap it in `CanvasTexture` for dynamic labels, minimaps or procedural patterns; call `texture.needsUpdate = true` after each redraw, and keep them small.

## Memory
Texture memory is width × height × 4 bytes × ~1.33 (mips). A 2048² texture is ~22 MB on the GPU, no matter how small its file. Budget by that number, and compress (KTX2) for anything large.

title: 14 · Interaction and controls
07 · Entities, components and systems
09 · Performance
text:
# 09 · Performance

Target **60 fps on the weakest device you care about**. Measure first, change one thing, measure again.

## Know the budget
Per frame at 60 fps you have **16.6 ms**, shared between your code, the browser, and the GPU. Aim to use ~10 ms so spikes don't drop frames.

## Find the bottleneck before fixing anything
| Symptom | Likely cause | First test |
|---|---|---|
| FPS rises a lot when you shrink the window | **Fill-rate / pixel-bound** (heavy shaders, big transparents, high DPR) | Lower `setPixelRatio` |
| FPS unchanged by window size, CPU thread pegged | **CPU-bound** (too many draw calls, heavy JS) | Check `renderer.info.render.calls` |
| Periodic hitches every few seconds | **Garbage collection** | Look for per-frame allocations |
| Hitch when something first appears | **Shader compile / texture upload** | Pre-warm: render it once off-screen at load |

## The big wins, in order
1. **Cut draw calls.** Aim for under ~300. Merge static geometry, share materials, use `InstancedMesh` for repeats.
2. **Cap resolution.** `min(devicePixelRatio, 2)`, and offer a quality slider that drops to 1.
3. **Fewer, cheaper lights and shadows.** One shadow-casting light; bake the rest.
4. **Cull.** Frustum culling is automatic; add distance culling and room/zone visibility for large worlds.
5. **LOD.** Swap to cheaper meshes or billboards at distance.
6. **Texture memory.** Use compressed (KTX2) textures; downscale anything that never appears large.

## Don't allocate in the hot path
Creating `new Vector3()` or `{}` every frame feeds the garbage collector and causes hitches.
```js
const tmp = new THREE.Vector3();          // allocate once, reuse
function update() { tmp.copy(a).sub(b).normalize(); }
```
Pool short-lived things (bullets, particles, damage numbers): keep an array of inactive objects, grab one, reset it, return it when done.

## Update less often what you can
Run AI at 10 Hz, not 60. Update far-away entities every few frames. Sleep entities with nothing to do.

## Particles
Use one `Points` or `InstancedMesh` for thousands of particles and animate them in the vertex shader from a start time and seed. Simulating each in JS doesn't scale.

## Measure on a real low-end device
A mid-range phone shows problems your desktop hides. Test early, and test on the slowest target regularly, not once at the end.

## Build a quality ladder
Low / Medium / High presets that change pixel ratio, shadow size, particle counts and draw distance. Auto-select by measuring the first few seconds of frame time, and let the player override.
